sourceLesson: Backend LLD: Concurrency-1: Processes, Threads and the GIL

questions.title: GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) actually guarantee?
questions.question: What does the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) actually guarantee?

options.optionText: That your shared variables will always update correctly across threads
That only one thread can execute Python bytecode at a time, and each individual bytecode instruction runs without interruption
That threads always run in the order they were started
That CPU-bound tasks will run faster with more threads

questions.title: Two threads both run this function, then the final value is printed:
questions.question:
Two threads both run this function, then the final value is printed:

```python
counter = 0
def increment():
    global counter
    for _ in range(1_000_000):
        counter += 1
```

What is the most likely printed value after both threads finish?

options.optionText: Always exactly 2,000,000
Always exactly 1,000,000
Some number less than 2,000,000, and it may differ each time the program runs
The program crashes with a RuntimeError

questions.title: scenario in H2 happen
questions.question: Why does the scenario in H2 happen even though the GIL only lets one thread run at a time?

options.optionText: counter += 1 is actually four separate bytecode steps, and the GIL can switch threads between those steps, not just between lines
The GIL doesn't apply to loops
global variables are not protected by the GIL at all
Python re-runs the loop twice by mistake

questions.title: threading and multiprocessing
questions.question: A student wants to speed up a task that makes 5 slow network API calls (each takes 1 second, mostly spent waiting). They're deciding between threading and multiprocessing. What should they pick, and why?

options.optionText: multiprocessing, because it always beats threading for any task
threading, because I/O-bound waits release the GIL, letting waits overlap — cheaper than spinning up separate processes
Neither will help; only rewriting the API calls can speed this up
multiprocessing, because network calls are CPU-bound

questions.title: difference in output/behavior
questions.question: What is the key difference in output/behavior between using raw multiprocessing.Process objects versus multiprocessing.Pool.map() for running the same function on 4 inputs?

options.optionText: Process automatically collects and returns results in a list; Pool.map() does not
Pool.map() runs the function sequentially, while Process runs it in parallel
Process requires manually creating, starting, and joining each process with no built-in result collection, while Pool.map() handles all of that and returns results in order automatically
There is no real difference; Pool is just a shorter way to write Process

questions.title: difference between concurrency and parallelism?
questions.question: What is the main difference between concurrency and parallelism?

options.optionText: Concurrency needs multiple CPU cores; parallelism doesn't
Concurrency is switching between tasks to make progress on all of them; parallelism is tasks actually running at the same instant
They are the same thing, just different names
Parallelism only applies to Python; concurrency applies to all languages

questions.title: What will this print?
questions.question:
What will this print?

```python
t1 = threading.Thread(target=notify_driver, args=("D101",))
t1.start()
print("Main thread is done!")
```

options.optionText: "Main thread is done!" always prints after notify_driver finishes
notify_driver never runs because .join() was skipped
This code throws an error because .join() was not called
"Main thread is done!" prints almost immediately, likely before notify_driver finishes

questions.title: what does .join() do?
questions.question: In Python's threading module, what does .join() do?

options.optionText: Merges two threads into one
Starts a thread that was created but not yet running
Pauses the calling code until that specific thread has finished
Kills the thread immediately

questions.title: A student wrote:
questions.question:
A student wrote:
```python
t1 = threading.Thread(target=notify_driver, args=("D101"))
t1.start()
```
This crashes with a TypeError about arguments not being iterable correctly. What's the mistake?

options.optionText: target should be a string, not a function reference
args is missing a trailing comma — ("D101") is just a string, not a one-item tuple, so Python tries to unpack each character as a separate argument
.start() must be called before target is assigned
notify_driver cannot accept any arguments

questions.title: Given a single CPU-bound function
questions.question: Given a single CPU-bound function cpu_heavy() that takes 4 seconds to run alone, what is the most likely total time if it's run twice using two threading.Thread instances (started and joined) on a machine with free cores?

options.optionText: About 8 seconds — roughly the same as running both sequentially, since the GIL prevents real parallel CPU execution
About 4 seconds total, since threads run in true parallel
About 2 seconds (threads split the CPU work evenly)
Less than 1 second, since threads always speed up computation
